45:A trader holding a return-predicting signal must weigh the gain a forecast promises against the cost of realizing it and the risk of holding it, acting on current information alone. The problem is a quadratic optimization: the gain of the position against the return, net of three frictions --- temporary impact, transient impact through a propagator kernel, and mean--variance inventory risk. The friction operator is non-local in time, so the unconstrained optimum needs the signal's future, and adaptedness is the binding constraint. Existing treatments characterize the adapted optimum implicitly, as the solution of an integral equation or an equivalent forward--backward system. Using a Wiener--Hopf factorization of the friction into causal and anticausal parts, we compute it in closed form away from horizon boundaries, by whitening the forecast, projecting onto the past, and recolouring. For a stationary Gaussian signal this is an explicit linear \emph{trading filter}. It reduces to the Markowitz rule under risk alone and, under pure power-law impact, to a fractional derivative of the signal of order $\nu=(1-\beta)/2$ with $\beta$ the impact exponent; rational frictions give filters with finitely many exponential moving averages, recovering the G\^arleanu--Pedersen aim portfolio and the stationary Neuman--Vo\ss{} solution. The causal factor on the imaginary axis yields a closed-form value of information, a causality gap $\sin(\pi\beta/2)$ under power-law impact, and a rate response that identifies when the optimum trades against its own transient impact. On a finite horizon the factors become terminal-anchored Gohberg--Krein factors, recovering the Gatheral--Schied--Slynko and Forde--S\'anchez-Betancourt--Smith solutions. ### B1 — Value figure: baked-in title contradicts caption and body text
